title: Mathematical Model of VCOs
intro: To analyse a PLL the VCO is described by what it does to phase: it integrates the control voltage (Razavi, Section 15.5).

blocks.text: Phase and frequency

In $V_m\sin\phi(t)$, $\phi$ is the total phase; the waveform crosses zero whenever $\phi$ passes a multiple of $\pi$. A signal whose phase climbs faster crosses zero more often, so frequency is the slope of phase:
A phase that alternates between two slopes produces a waveform that alternates between two frequencies, which is binary frequency modulation (frequency shift keying).
The VCO output
Since $\omega_{out} = \omega_0 + K_{VCO}V_{cont}$ is memoryless, a change in $V_{cont}$ changes the frequency at once, and the phase integrates it:

(If the characteristic is nonlinear, $K_{VCO}$ cannot be pulled out of the integral.) Writing $V_m\cos[(\omega_0 + K_{VCO}V_{cont})t]$ instead is a common mistake: differentiating that phase gives an extra term $K_{VCO}t\,dV_{cont}/dt$, which is wrong unless $V_{cont}$ is constant.
Excess phase and the integrator model
In a PLL only the second term matters. Call it the excess phase $\phi_{ex} = K_{VCO}\int V_{cont}dt$; viewed from control voltage to excess phase, the VCO is an ideal integrator:
This pole at the origin is why a PLL with any loop filter has at least one integrator in its loop.
Ripple on the control line
Let $V_{cont} = V_m\cos\omega_m t$. Then $V_{out} = V_0\cos\left(\omega_0 t + \frac{K_{VCO}V_m}{\omega_m}\sin\omega_m t\right)$. For a small modulation index ($K_{VCO}V_m/\omega_m \ll 1$ rad):

blocks.alt: A spectrum with a tall line at omega0 and two shorter lines at omega0 minus omegam and omega0 plus omegam.
blocks.caption: A small periodic disturbance on $V_{cont}$ creates sidebands at $\omega_0 \pm \omega_m$, each $K_{VCO}V_m/(2\omega_m)$ relative to the carrier.

blocks.text: So a VCO is also a frequency modulator, and in a locked loop the control voltage must be very quiet; any periodic ripple appears as spurs beside the carrier (reference spurs in a PLL).
Non-sinusoidal outputs

A square-ish output is a Fourier series. If the fundamental's frequency moves by $\Delta f$, the $n$th harmonic moves by $n\Delta f$, so the $n$th term carries $nK_{VCO}\int V_{cont}dt$ of excess phase. The harmonics follow the fundamental, so analysis usually tracks the fundamental only, even when waveforms are drawn as rectangles.
Jitter and phase noise

A real oscillator's zero crossings wander. Writing the output as $A\cos[\omega_0 t + \phi_n(t)]$, the random $\phi_n(t)$ is jitter in the time domain; its spectrum is phase noise in the frequency domain. Phase noise is usually quoted as the noise power in a 1 Hz band at an offset $\Delta\omega$ from the carrier, relative to the carrier power, in dBc/Hz. It falls with offset, and for a given oscillator improves with larger swing and, for LC designs, higher tank Q. The PLL page shows how a loop suppresses the slow part of this wander.

blocks.title: Phase from a frequency step
blocks.text: A VCO with $K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 100\text{ MHz/V}$ sees $V_{cont}$ rise by 50 mV for 10 ns and then return. How much extra phase has it accumulated?
solution: The frequency returns to its old value but the phase offset remains: phase is the integral of frequency.

blocks.title: Sideband level
blocks.text: $K_{VCO} = 2\pi \times 200\text{ MHz/V}$ and the control line carries a 1 mV, 1 MHz ripple. Find the modulation index and the sideband level relative to the carrier.
solution: Index $K_{VCO}V_m/\omega_m = (2\pi \cdot 2\times10^8 \cdot 10^{-3})/(2\pi \cdot 10^6) = 0.2\text{ rad}$, small enough for the approximation.
Each sideband is half the index: 0.1 of the carrier, i.e. $-20\text{ dBc}$.

blocks.title: FSK
blocks.text: A VCO with $f_0 = 1\text{ GHz}$ and $K_{VCO} = 50\text{ MHz/V}$ (i.e. $2\pi \times 50$ Mrad/s/V) has $V_{cont}$ toggling between 0 and 0.1 V. What two frequencies does it produce, and what does the phase look like?
solution: 1 GHz and $1\text{ GHz} + 50\text{ MHz/V} \times 0.1\text{ V} = 1.005\text{ GHz}$.
The phase is a continuous ramp whose slope alternates between $2\pi \times 1.000$ and $2\pi \times 1.005$ Grad/s; there are no phase jumps.

blocks.title: Harmonics
blocks.text: A ring VCO's square-wave output has its fundamental pulled 10 MHz higher by the control voltage. How far do the third and fifth harmonics move?
solution: The $n$th harmonic carries $n$ times the excess phase, so it moves by $n \times 10\text{ MHz}$: 30 MHz and 50 MHz.
